title: Spider-Man Debuted in the Final Issue of a Comic That Was Being Cancelled
excerpt:
Amazing Fantasy #15 introduced Peter Parker in August 1962.
Unexpected sales success turned a last-chance experiment into a Marvel landmark.
body_md:
Spider-Man's first appearance came under circumstances that hardly suggested the birth of a global entertainment icon. Amazing Fantasy #15, published in August 1962, was the final issue of a struggling anthology series.

The publication had previously been known as Amazing Adventures and Amazing Adult Fantasy, presenting short science-fiction stories aimed largely at adult readers. Poor sales led publisher Martin Goodman to cancel the title.

That impending cancellation gave Stan Lee and Steve Ditko an opportunity to introduce an unconventional hero. Peter Parker was a teenager dealing with ordinary personal problems, rather than an adult superhero or a youthful sidekick.

The concept initially faced skepticism, but the doomed anthology provided a relatively low-risk place to try it. Spider-Man appeared prominently on the cover of the last issue.

Although the anthology ended as planned, its sales results surprised the publisher. The character's popularity led to The Amazing Spider-Man #1 and eventually to one of Marvel's most enduring franchises.

The origin of Spider-Man as a publishing gamble is a reminder that an apparently unsuccessful project can sometimes provide the setting for a breakthrough idea.
